A 61-point comparative due-diligence review, with measured terrain analysis, regulatory research and construction-cost modelling.

Waterpointe subdivision, Unit 3 Lot 23 · 1.330 acres, vacant · fronts J.W. Smith Reservoir
Parcel 05050A A003 · Zoning RS-180 · Unincorporated Clayton County Official
33.416191°N, 84.369848°W · Census Tract 13063040636
Property B 1147 & 1153 Watersedge Cove, Lots 130 & 131, Tignall, GA 30668
Stillwater Coves subdivision · 2.14 acres (two 1.07-ac lots), vacant · near Clarks Hill / J. Strom Thurmond Lake
APN 10A 130 · MLS 98224174 · Asking $55,000 (both lots) · Lincoln County Official
33.941877°N, 82.564164°W · Census Tract 13181970100
Both addresses are in a different county than the mailing address implies Property A is not in Henry County and the lake is not a Henry County Water Authority reservoir; Property B is not in Wilkes County. Both corrections were verified independently against the US Census Bureau geocoder and the counties' own GIS. They change the zoning, septic, permitting, tax and short-term-rental rules that apply. See §0.

How the county corrections were established

PropertyEvidenceSource
A Census Bureau geocoder, coordinate query at 33.416191, −84.369848 returns Counties: Clayton County and no Incorporated Place at all (= unincorporated). County Subdivision Jonesboro CCD. Official geocoding.geo.census.gov
The parcel is present in Clayton County's own tax assessor parcel service with PARCELID 05050A A003, ZONE RS180, UNIT 3, LOT 23, NEIGHBORHOODDESC WATERPOINTE. A Henry County parcel could not appear there. Official gis.claytoncountyga.gov
CCWA's own fishing page states "J.W. Smith Reservoir is a 250 acre CCWA-owned lake." HCWA's reservoir page lists its complete five-reservoir network — Tussahaw, Upper Towaliga, Lower Towaliga, Long Branch, Indian Creek/Gardner — and J.W. Smith is not among them. Official ccwa.us / hcwa.com
The Waterpointe HOA's own bylaws place the subdivision in "Land Lots 50, 51, 78 & 79 of the 5th District of Clayton County, Georgia" and record that in 1992 "jurisdictional authority was transferred to Clayton County." Official waterpointehoa.com
B Census Bureau geocoder at 33.941877, −82.564164 returns Counties: Lincoln County, County Subdivision Lincolnton CCD, Tract 9701. Official geocoding.geo.census.gov
The recorded Declaration of Covenants for Stillwater Coves was filed in Lincoln County Superior Court, 15 June 2006 (Deed Book 165, pp. 246–293). The developer's own site says "historic Lincoln County." Official stillwatercovesgeorgia.com
Tax APN on the MLS record reads 10A 130, Lincoln County; schools assigned are Lincoln County Elementary / Middle / High. Listing
Why the confusion is understandable Property A's mailing address is genuinely "Hampton, GA 30228" and Hampton is a Henry County city — but the lot sits in the Clayton County "panhandle," a southern salient of Clayton County that reaches down toward Hampton. This is also why the subdivision is reached from Panhandle Road. Property B's "Tignall, GA 30668" is a Wilkes County post office serving a Lincoln County parcel. In both cases the USPS address and the governing jurisdiction differ.

An incidental confirmation: a FEMA FIRM panel query at Property A's coordinates returns panels for both 13063C (Clayton) and 13151C (Henry) — the lot is close enough to the county line that both county map panels cover the point. The Clayton panel (13063C0165F) is the governing one.

Executive summary

The findings that decide these two lots

Everything below is expanded, sourced and quantified in the body of the report.
1 Property A is not a recreational lake lot. It is a view lot on a closed drinking-water reservoir. J.W. Smith Reservoir is a raw drinking-water supply owned by CCWA. CCWA's published rules: boats capped at 20 ft, electric motors or paddles only — "gas motor usage is prohibited under any circumstances"; "access to the reservoir shall be made only at the entrance gate"; "wading, swimming, or bathing is prohibited." Open Sat–Wed only, 1 Mar – 31 Oct, on a paid permit. No private dock programme exists. And the lot does not touch the water — CCWA owns the bed, the shoreline and a measured ~33-ft strip between the rear lot line and the waterline. Official GIS-derived

At least one MLS listing in this subdivision advertises "private access to lake." CCWA's Rule 5 contradicts it.
2 Property B is marketed as "DOCKABLE." That claim is unsubstantiated and the price says so. The MLS remarks assert both lots are dockable, but the structured MLS waterfront field reads "Lake Privileges" — not a dock or dock permit. Sibling listings in the same subdivision enumerate the dockable lots as 125, 128 and 140 (and 24, 26, 35, 103); 130 and 131 appear in none of them. On the same street, lots marketed as dockable ask $136,000–$143,250 each; the subject pair asks $55,000 for two acres — roughly a 5× per-acre discount. Price history: $149,000 (Mar 2024) › $49,900 (Apr 2025) › $55,000 (Jun 2026), −63%. Listing

USACE is explicit that only a ranger's on-site field inspection determines dockability, that it is first-come first-served, and that permits "will not be issued for commercial or speculative purposes in order to enhance the selling potential of adjacent private property." Official
3 We measured Property B's low point at 26 ft above full pool, and the nearest full-pool water at ~199 ft away. Working from the 1-metre lidar DEM: within the reconstructed 2.14-acre footprint the lowest ground is 356.0 ft against a 330.0 ft full pool. The nearest ground at or below 330 ft lies ~199 ft beyond the lot, across land that is federal fee property (the USACE purchase boundary was set at elevation 346 ft). So there is a real band of Corps land between the lot and the water, and the final descent to the shore is the steepest ground in the whole transect — 27.4% over 50 ft (15.3°). GIS-derived Boundary requires a licensed survey
4 Property A's slope is materially steeper than the listing describes. One listing calls it a "perfect gentle rolling lot." Listing The lidar says otherwise: 81.7 ft of relief across the lot, an in-lot average grade of 18.4% (10.4°), and a maximum of 25.6% (14.3°) over a 50-ft run immediately below the road. That is a moderate-to-steep building site requiring engineered grading, almost certainly retaining structures, and a stepped or daylight-basement foundation. GIS-derived

Property B is the opposite: in-lot average 3.7% (2.1°), max 7.3% over 50 ft — genuinely gently sloping, exactly as its listing claims. On buildability of the pad itself, Property B wins clearly.
5 A zoning provision exists that was written for Property A's reservoir by name. Clayton County Zoning Sec. 4.5(D), "J.W. Smith Reservoir" requires lots abutting the reservoir to be >=50,000 SF with >=400 ft depth, imposes a permanent 150-ft protection buffer in which no septic tank, absorption field, related structure or substantial structure may sit, and states "sanitary sewer to be installed unless EPD indicates such sewer should not be installed." Official

The lot passes both numeric tests (57,954 SF, ~416 ft deep, measured). The buffer consumes roughly 36% of the lot depth, leaving about 237 ft of usable depth — a real but manageable constraint. Whether sewer or septic governs is unresolved and is the single most consequential open question on Property A.
6 Both soils are rated "Very limited" for septic — for different reasons, and Property B's is worse. USDA NRCS rates the septic-absorption suitability of both sites "Very limited" (1.00). Official
  • A — Gwinnett sandy clay loam (GwE2), 10–25% slopes: limited by slope (1.00), depth to paralithic bedrock at 50 in (0.77) and slow percolation (0.50). Hydrologic group B, low shrink–swell (LEP 1.5%).
  • B — Zion silt loam (ZnE), 10–25% slopes: limited by indurated lithic bedrock at only 30 in (1.00) and slope (1.00). Hydrologic group C, saturated conductivity as low as 2 µm/s, and LEP 7.5% — high shrink–swell. Surface erodibility K = 0.43.
Zion's 30-inch hard rock is the single most dangerous soil fact in this report. Georgia requires 24 in of clean vertical separation below a drainfield trench; with rock at 30 in the margin is almost nil. A conventional 5-bedroom drainfield may not be permittable in Zion soil at all. Requires a soil-classifier evaluation and perc test
7 Flood risk is genuinely low at both — the only unambiguously clean finding. FEMA's National Flood Hazard Layer returns Zone X — "Area of Minimal Flood Hazard" at both coordinates, SFHA = False, no Base Flood Elevation published, no floodway. Panels 13063C0165F (eff. 7 Jun 2017) and 13181C0050B (eff. 17 Apr 2020). Neither lot is in a Special Flood Hazard Area, so no federal flood-insurance mandate and no minimum finished-floor elevation flows from FEMA. Official
Both counties are also Piedmont crystalline bedrock — no karst, no sinkhole risk.

›The two things that most separate these properties

Property A wins on
  • Schools 1.8 miles away — Michelle Obama STEM Elementary and Eddie White Middle are both at 11808 Panhandle Rd; Lovejoy High 3.8 mi. Property B: all three schools 18.1 mi / ~41 min each way, for 13 years.
  • Emergency department ~22 min (Piedmont Fayette); four EDs within 35 min; Level I trauma ~45 min. Property B: nearest ED ~45 min at a small rural hospital; Level I trauma ~98 min; nearest urgent care ~49 min, in South Carolina.
  • Hartsfield-Jackson 21 mi / ~43 min, ~220 nonstop destinations, with a MARTA rail link. Property B: ATL is 135 mi / ~3h15m.
  • Hindu Temple of Atlanta 17.7 mi / ~32 min, in the same county; 3 Indian restaurants within 30 min; ~15,000–30,000 Asian Indian residents within an hour. Property B's nearest Hindu temple is 81.7 mi / ~2h23m, in another state; no gurdwara within 100 mi.
  • Groceries 2.9 mi, Walmart 4.3 mi, hardware 4.9 mi. Property B is 3×–10× further on every category; no grocery, pharmacy, bank or fuel within 14 miles.
  • Affluent immediate area: tract median household income $119,872 vs county $59,806.
Property B wins on
  • A genuinely usable lake. Clarks Hill / Thurmond is 71,100 acres with ~1,200 miles of shoreline, no horsepower or motor restrictions, open year-round, with marinas and public ramps. This is the real difference: A's water body is legally closed to meaningful recreation; B's is one of the largest reservoirs in the eastern United States.
  • A gentle, easily buildable pad — 3.7% average grade across the lot, vs 18.4% at A.
  • Small schools: student–teacher ratios 13.6–15.5 vs 16.9–21.7; a high school of 367 students vs Lovejoy's 2,136.
  • Twice the land (2.14 ac vs 1.33 ac) for less than half the price ($55,000 vs a $125,000 asking / $85,000 last sale).
  • Quiet. Atlanta Motor Speedway is 7.5 mi / ~17 min from Property A — inside the audible envelope of NASCAR Cup weekends, with race-day traffic on the same two-lane roads the lot depends on.
  • Lower radon potential (Zone 3 vs Zone 2) and no reservoir-buffer overlay.

›Construction cost for a 5-bedroom home — the headline answer

ScenarioA — 3,500 SF heated, 5 BRB — 3,100 SF heated, 5 BR
Low$575,800  ($164/SF)$621,000  ($200/SF)
Likely$833,600  ($238/SF)$940,600  ($303/SF)
Practical high (~80th pct)~$1,060,000  ($303/SF)~$1,223,000  ($394/SF)
Best local finished comparable$565,000$422,000
Build cost as % of comp148%223%
Paper loss before paying for land~ $269,000~ $519,000
The counter-intuitive result, and it is robust The smaller house on the cheaper land costs about $107,000 more to build — $65/SF more. Drivers in order of size: fixed site costs spread over less floor area ($43/SF of site cost at B vs $31/SF at A); a ~$59,000 rural mobilisation premium; longer driveway, water line and power run plus a propane system A does not need; covenant-mandated premium materials (standing-seam metal roof, ~900 SF of deep porch); and higher overhead, profit and contingency justified by a thin bidder pool and a 15-month covenant deadline to complete construction. Estimate

In Waterpointe, $541,000–$565,000 already buys a finished large home against $833,600 to build one — a saving of roughly $280,000 for substantially the same product. If the objective is a large house at or near its cost, buying beats building at both locations, and by a wide margin at B.
The decision in one paragraph These are not two versions of the same thing. Property A is a steep, well-serviced, well-schooled metro-fringe lot with excellent access to hospitals, an airport and a South Asian community — whose "lakefront" is a legal fiction for recreational purposes. Property B is a gentle, cheap, remote lot on a magnificent real lake — whose waterfront status, dock rights and septic capacity are all unproven, and whose distance from schools and emergency medicine is permanent and unfixable. If anyone in the household is school-age, elderly, medically vulnerable, flies often, or wants South Asian community access, Property A is in a different category. Property B makes sense only for a buyer whose central purpose is lake recreation and solitude — and only after USACE confirms in writing, for Lots 130 and 131 specifically, that a dock is possible. Until that letter exists, Property B should be valued as a lake-view lot, not a lakefront one.

The plat date is not a formality here. USACE Thurmond SMP ¶16.a provides that in county-certified subdivisions platted on or after 1 May 2018, only community docks will be authorised. The 2006 covenants suggest the subdivision predates that — but the plat (or any replat) for the Watersedge Cove phase must be dated from the Lincoln County plat book before relying on any individual-dock possibility.

4GIS / aerial parcel mapping and discrepancy analysis

Discrepancies identified between GIS, plat, listing and our measurements

#DiscrepancyDetail and our assessment
D1A Which line is the frontage A secondary analysis of this parcel reported ~147.5 ft of frontage on Edgewater Drive and ~129.8 ft at the rear. That is reversed. We established orientation three independent ways: (i) the C4/C5 corners lie 18.5 and 24.9 ft from the Edgewater Drive centreline while C1/C2 lie 434.7 and 453.8 ft away; (ii) C3–C5 stand at 888–892 ft elevation and C1–C2 at 810–814 ft, and the subdivision road runs along the ridge; (iii) the NAIP imagery shows the road to the north and the water to the south. Road frontage is the 130.3 ft line; the 148.1 ft line faces the reservoir. GIS-derived
D2A "Gentle rolling lot" The listing's characterisation is contradicted by 1-metre lidar: 81.7 ft of relief, 18.4% average in-lot grade, 25.6% maximum over 50 ft. See §7. Treat the listing's topography language as marketing.
D3A "Private access to lake" An MLS listing for a neighbouring Waterpointe lot advertises private lake access. CCWA Rule 5 states access "shall be made only at the entrance gate," and Rule 8 prohibits wading, swimming or bathing. The two cannot both be true. Official
D4A RS-180 lot-depth ratio RS-180 caps lot depth at 2.5 × lot width › 2.5 × 130.3 = 326 ft maximum, yet the lot is ~416 ft deep; and Sec. 4.5(D)(2) separately requires >=400 ft of depth for lots abutting this reservoir. These two provisions are mathematically irreconcilable for any lot narrower than 160 ft. The lot was platted in 1988, so it is almost certainly a lawful non-conforming lot of record — but get that confirmed in writing. Official Needs a zoning determination
D5A Where the 150-ft buffer is measured from Sec. 4.5(D)(3) says the buffer adjoins "the reservoir property" (= the rear lot line); Sec. 4.6(E) says adjoining the reservoir property "from the normal full-pool elevation" (~33 ft further out). The difference is ~4,400 sq ft of lot. Sec. 4.6(E)'s own conflict rule says the more restrictive standard governs, so assume measurement from the rear lot line. Official
D6A Asking price $125,000 vs $98,000 reported by different aggregators, against a $60,000 county appraisal and an $85,000 August 2021 sale. Establish the actual current price and status with the listing broker. Listing
D7B "DOCKABLE" Asserted in the remarks; contradicted by the structured "Lake Privileges" field, by sibling listings that enumerate dockable lots without 130/131, by the ~5× per-acre price discount, and by the absence of any claimed permit. The single most important item to resolve. See §26.
D8B Price: owner vs MLS Owner's HOA advert, Feb 2025: $110,000 for both. MLS, Apr 2025: $49,900 for both; now $55,000. A 2.2× gap within two months. Listing
D9B Road frontage type MLS records "Road Frontage Type: City Street, State Road" for an interior subdivision cul-de-sac. Implausible — almost certainly a data-entry error. Watersedge Cove is a private or subdivision street. Listing
D10B Address-point geometry The Esri geocoder places 1105–1177 Watersedge Cove as 13 perfectly evenly spaced points 99.8 ft apart on a line whose bearing (60.6°) differs from the mapped road centreline (75.3°), drifting from 2 m off the road at 1105 to 267 ft off at 1147. These are interpolated address points, not surveyed building sites. We used the along-street station but not the lateral offset. GIS-derived
D11B Which "frontage" is 198 ft MLS gives "Frontage Type: Lakefront; Frontage Length: 198.0 ft". For a waterfront listing this normally means water frontage, but 198 ft is also exactly 2 × the 99.8 ft address-point spacing, which suggests road frontage. Unresolved without the plat; our reconstruction assumes 99 ft of road frontage per lot. Not found
D12B County of record Listing portals index the property under "Tignall, GA 30668," a Wilkes County post office. The parcel is in Lincoln County. Affects every regulatory enquiry. Official
How Property B's boundary was reconstructed — and the limits of it Because no plat or parcel polygon is obtainable, Figure A-5's lot outline is a reconstruction built from: the OpenStreetMap-traced Watersedge Cove centreline (verified against NAIP imagery); the along-street stations of the 1147 and 1153 address points projected perpendicularly onto that centreline; a lot width of 99 ft (from the 198-ft MLS frontage ÷ 2, corroborated by the 99.8-ft address-point spacing); a depth of 471 ft solved from the stated 1.07-acre area; and an axis perpendicular to the road (bearing 345.3°). Estimate

It reproduces the stated area to within 0.4% (2.149 ac measured vs 2.14 ac stated), which is reassuring but not probative. The shape could be materially different — lake-subdivision lots are frequently pie-shaped or follow the shoreline. Every distance-to-water figure in this report for Property B therefore carries the reconstruction's uncertainty, and must be re-derived from the recorded plat and a boundary survey. Survey required

Interpretation. Even allowing generously for reconstruction error, the lot does not reach the water. There is a band of land — on the evidence, federal fee land — between the rear lot line and the lake, and at winter pool the walk to water's edge is of the order of 400+ ft. That is entirely normal for a Thurmond Lake lot and not by itself a defect; USACE acquired to elevation 346 ft everywhere. But it does mean "direct waterfront access" describes a right to walk across public land, not ownership of frontage — and it is why the dock question in §26 is decisive rather than incidental.

Reading the two sections together — the single most useful comparison in this report Property A has 90 ft of fall in 507 ft, all of it on the lot. Property B has 60 ft of fall in 884 ft, almost none of it on the lot. The two maximum 50-ft grades are nearly identical (25.6% vs 27.4%) — but on Property A the steepest ground is where you have to build, and on Property B it is on land you will never build on.

Put plainly: Property A's slope is a construction problem. Property B's slope is a walk to the water. If the steep reach on Property B deters you, the answer is a path or steps across the federal strip — subject to a USACE licence, since improved walkways require one and are not permitted in Protected Shoreline areas. On Property A the answer is retaining walls and engineered fill measured in tens of thousands of dollars.

Property A: what the slope actually costs 18.4% average grade over a 416-ft-deep lot, combined with the 150-ft rear buffer that pushes the building envelope uphill into the steepest third, is the central engineering problem on this property. The practical consequences, all of which belong in a build budget:
  • An engineered cut-and-fill pad, with the cut on the uphill (road) side and fill downhill
  • Retaining structures — segmental block or engineered wall — almost certainly required; anything over 4 ft high needs engineered design and a permit
  • A stepped or daylight-basement foundation is the economical answer to this slope, and happens also to be the one that suits a lake-view lot
  • Septic on an 18% slope is already rated "Very limited" by NRCS specifically because of slope; trenches must run on contour, which constrains where the house can sit
  • Driveway grade, drainage, culverts and a turnaround
  • Georgia land-disturbance permitting and an E&S plan — in a water-supply watershed

8Three-dimensional terrain models

Property A — slope direction and exposure

Aspect is due south (170.7°) — the lot faces the water and the sun. Practical effects: excellent passive-solar and daylight potential for a lake-facing house; strong afternoon heat gain on west-facing glazing; a south-facing slope dries fastest after rain, which helps construction access but accelerates runoff straight toward the reservoir. All surface water from this lot discharges into a public drinking-water supply, which is precisely why the 150-ft buffer and the watershed ordinance exist.

Property B — slope direction and exposure

Aspect is due north (352.8°) at a gentle 6.4%. A north aspect means the lake view is to the north, so a lake-facing house gets soft indirect light rather than direct sun on its main elevation — pleasant in a Georgia summer, and worth knowing before orienting the plan. North slopes hold moisture longer and dry more slowly, which matters for a drainfield in a hydrologic-group-C soil. The gentle grade means runoff is slow, which is good for erosion and bad for shedding water away from a slab — positive drainage away from the house will need to be designed, not assumed.

What Zone X means in practice for both lots
  • No federal flood-insurance purchase requirement for a federally backed mortgage. Insurance remains available and inexpensive under a Preferred Risk Policy, and is worth buying on a lake lot regardless.
  • No FEMA-driven minimum finished-floor elevation, because there is no Base Flood Elevation at either site. Any minimum floor elevation will come from the building code (positive drainage away from the structure), the county, or good practice — not from the floodplain ordinance. See §13.
  • No floodplain-development permit triggered, and no Elevation Certificate required.
  • Both findings are consistent with the measured topography: Property A's low point stands 8.6 ft above the reservoir's normal surface and Property B's stands 26 ft above full pool. Neither lot is plausibly inundated by the 1% flood.
Two flood-adjacent risks that FEMA maps do not show Property A — dam hazard classification. The J.W. Smith dam is classed "High hazard" in the National Inventory of Dams (GA03893) — meaning failure "will probably cause loss of human life" downstream. The subject lot is upstream-adjacent, i.e. beside the impoundment and not in the failure inundation path, so this is not a direct risk to the parcel. The official inundation mapping sits in the dam's Emergency Action Plan, held by CCWA and the Georgia Safe Dams Program. Last recorded inspection January 2016, condition "Satisfactory". Official

Property B — reservoir operating range, not flooding. Thurmond Lake is actively regulated. Full pool is 330 ft; normal winter pool is 326 ft (15 Oct – 15 Dec), returning to 330 ft Jan–May. Drought operations go lower: the lake registered 324.28 ft in Dec 2025 (drought trigger L1) and 322.05 ft in Jan 2026 (L2), and stood at 319.96 ft on 7 Oct 2026 — about 10 ft below full pool. Official — USACE This is not a flood risk; it is a usability risk, and it is the reason the SMP allows permittees to "chase water." It also means right now is close to an ideal time to inspect this lot, because the shoreline is as exposed as it gets.

13Minimum finished-floor elevation

Because there is no BFE, the usual arithmetic does not apply — and we will not invent one The requested calculation is estimated BFE + required freeboard = minimum finished-floor elevation. With no BFE at either property, that equation has no inputs. Georgia's floodplain freeboard requirements (commonly BFE + 1 ft to + 3 ft depending on the local ordinance) apply only within a Special Flood Hazard Area. Neither lot is in one. Official

Per the brief's instruction, we have specifically not assumed that fill is permitted. It mostly is not, in the places it would matter.
DeterminationProperty AProperty B
Minimum FFE from FEMA / floodplain rulesNone imposedNone imposed
Governing minimum instead International Residential Code (2024 edition, in force in Georgia) grading provisions — finished grade must fall away from the foundation, and the floor must sit above adjacent grade with positive drainage. No reservoir-driven floor elevation exists. Same IRC grading provisions. No USACE-driven floor elevation exists; USACE regulates only land below the 346-ft boundary, which the lot does not include.
Is the existing terrain adequate? Yes, for flood purposes — abundantly. The constraint here is slope, not elevation. Yes — 26 ft of freeboard above full pool on the lowest ground.
Is fill necessary? Not for flood reasons — but substantial cut-and-fill is needed to create a level building pad on an 18% grade. That is a grading problem, and it is regulated: Sec. 38-144.1(b) minimises grading and filling in stream setbacks, Sec. 4.6(A) requires the 150-ft buffer be "left in their natural undisturbed state," and a county land-disturbance permit with an erosion & sediment control plan will be required in a drinking-water supply watershed. Do not assume fill in the buffer is available at any price. No. Routine site preparation only.
Must the house be elevated?NoNo
Restrictions on slab / crawlspace / pier? None from floodplain rules. Real constraints come from (i) the 18% slope, which favours a stepped foundation or daylight basement; (ii) paralithic bedrock at ~50 in, which raises the cost of any deep excavation; (iii) NRCS rating "Very limited" for dwellings both with and without basements, on slope grounds. None from floodplain rules. Real constraints come from the soil: indurated lithic bedrock at ~30 in makes a basement impractical to impossible without rock excavation, and LEP 7.5% (high shrink–swell) in the Zion subsoil argues for a stiffened/post-tensioned slab or a crawlspace on properly prepared subgrade. NRCS also rates Zion "Very limited" for dwellings.
Freeboard we would nonetheless specify Not a flood matter, but on both lots we would set the finished floor at least 12–18 in above final adjacent grade with graded swales, and on Property A specifically design for uphill surface water interception — a cut-slope above a house on an 18% grade collects water that must be taken around the structure. Estimate — good practice

The Zion soil on Property B is the most serious technical finding in this report Three properties combine badly, and all three are official NRCS data:
  1. Indurated lithic bedrock at 77 cm (30 inches). "Indurated" means hard, unweathered rock — not the rippable saprolite typical of the Piedmont. Georgia's septic rule requires 24 inches of clean vertical separation below the trench bottom to rock. A conventional drainfield trench bottom sits roughly 18–30 in down. The arithmetic barely works, and often will not.
  2. Linear extensibility 7.5% in the Bt and Bt2. That is a high shrink–swell rating — expansive clay that moves with moisture. It is a foundation and slab-cracking risk and requires deliberate design.
  3. Ksat of 2 µm/s in the Bt and hydrologic group C. Water moves through this subsoil very slowly, which is exactly what a drainfield must not have.
NRCS accordingly rates Zion "Very limited" (1.00) for septic absorption fields, dwellings with and without basements, local roads, shallow excavations, small commercial buildings and lawns and landscaping. Every single engineering interpretation is "Very limited." Official

The mitigating fact: the lot area also contains Cecil sandy loam (CeB) on 2–6% slopes, which NRCS rates "Not limited" for dwellings and only "Somewhat limited" (0.498) for septic — a genuinely good soil. SSURGO is mapped at roughly 1:15,840 and cannot resolve which soil lies under a specific 2.14-acre lot. The commercial outcome of this purchase may turn entirely on whether the drainfield area is Zion or Cecil — and only a site soil evaluation by a Georgia-licensed soil classifier can answer that. Soil evaluation and perc test are mandatory pre-purchase items

A caution about reading these ratings "Very limited" in NRCS language means the soil has features unfavourable for the use and that overcoming them requires special design, significant extra cost or intensive maintenance. It does not mean prohibited. Houses are built on Gwinnett soils across metro Atlanta every day. For Property A the limitation is slope, which engineering solves with money. For Property B's Zion the limitation is 30-inch hard rock plus slope, and rock depth is the one constraint money cannot reliably solve for a septic drainfield — which is why the alternative soil (Cecil) on the same lot matters so much.

15Foundation suitability

Foundation typeProperty A — Gwinnett, 18% slope, rock at 50 inProperty B — Zion, 4% slope, hard rock at 30 in
Slab-on-grade Possible but expensive. Requires a large engineered cut-and-fill pad and retaining on the downhill side. Low shrink–swell (LEP 1.5%) is favourable for a slab; the slope is not. Feasible — with design for expansive clay. The gentle grade suits a slab, but LEP 7.5% argues for a stiffened or post-tensioned slab, or removal and replacement of the upper clay with engineered fill. A conventional thin slab on Zion Bt invites cracking.
Crawlspace Good fit. A crawlspace absorbs grade change cheaply and avoids a large pad. Requires proper venting/encapsulation and positive drainage on a slope that sheds water toward the structure from above. Probably the best choice. Keeps the structure off the expansive clay, needs only shallow excavation (staying above the 30-in rock), and allows services to be run and inspected.
Pier / beam Well suited to the downhill side of a sloping lot; minimises cut and site disturbance — valuable in a drinking-water watershed where disturbance is scrutinised. Workable; piers must bear below the active clay zone, and rock at 30 in limits pier depth — likely a shallow rock-bearing design.
Basement / daylight basement The natural solution to this lot. 81.7 ft of fall means a walk-out lower level is nearly free architecturally, turning the slope liability into lake-view living space. But: paralithic bedrock at ~50 in means a full basement excavation will meet weathered rock — rippable, not blast-requiring, but a real cost line. NRCS rates basements "Very limited." Impractical. Indurated lithic bedrock at 30 in would require rock excavation or blasting for any basement, and the gentle grade gives no daylight opportunity. Design for no basement.
Stepped foundation Strongly indicated. Stepped footings following the grade are the standard economical answer to an 18% slope and avoid mass earthworks. Not needed — grade does not require it.
Retaining walls Expect them. Engineered design and permit required above 4 ft. Budget accordingly; on a 25% local grade a terraced arrangement may be necessary. Not structurally required. Any low landscape wall is discretionary.
Geotechnical investigation advisable? Yes — strongly. Piedmont saprolite weathers in place and depth to competent rock varies dramatically over short distances (10 ft in one boring, 60 ft 50 ft away). Multiple borings across the actual footprint, plus slope-stability review given the 25% local grade. Yes — strongly, and for a different reason. You need to know (i) the true depth to the indurated contact across the footprint and the drainfield area, and (ii) the plasticity index / swell potential of the Bt clay. Combine the geotech with the soil-classifier evaluation for the septic permit.
The shared Piedmont caveat Both lots sit on Piedmont crystalline bedrock (§42). Ruling out sinkholes does not rule out geotechnical trouble: expect variable depth to rock, perched groundwater and seeps at the saprolite/rock interface (common on lake-adjacent slopes and directly relevant to both basement waterproofing and drainfield suitability), and rock near the surface driving up the cost of footings, utility trenches and especially septic trenches. Geotechnical investigation required

If a private well were needed: what is the ideal depth for good-quality water?

Well parameterProperty A — Clayton CountyProperty B — Lincoln County
AquiferPiedmont and Blue Ridge crystalline-rock aquifer (USGS national aquifer code N400PDMBRX) — confirmed for every USGS groundwater site in both counties Official
How water is producedNot from pore space but from fractures and joints in crystalline bedrock, overlain by saprolite. Yield depends on intersecting water-bearing fractures, so two wells 100 ft apart can differ by an order of magnitude.
Recorded well depths (USGS NWIS) Same aquifer system; county-specific distribution not tabulated here Median 190 ft; 25th–75th percentile 160–300 ft; maximum recorded 450 ft Official
Recommended target depth for reliable, good-quality water 200–400 ft, cased through the full saprolite and at least 20 ft into competent rock 200–350 ft, with 300–400 ft as the contingency budget
Why that depth Shallow saprolite wells are cheaper but are the ones that go dry in drought and are most exposed to surface contamination and septic influence. Going deeper into the fractured bedrock buys (i) a larger fracture catchment and so better drought resilience, (ii) a longer travel path from the surface, and (iii) storage in the borehole itself. Below roughly 400 ft in Piedmont rock, additional depth usually buys little extra yield — fracture density declines — and the risk of encountering mineralised water with elevated iron, manganese or radon rises. Lincoln County's drought frequency (60.9 events/yr in the FEMA NRI, the highest hazard frequency recorded for that county) is a direct argument for depth. Estimate from official inputs
Typical yield to design for5–15 gpm is normal for Piedmont domestic wells; a 5-bedroom house needs roughly 8–10 gpm or a smaller yield with storage. Below ~3 gpm, a storage tank and booster set become necessary.
Mandatory setbacks100 ft minimum from any septic drainfield (and from sinkholes); locate the well upgradient of the septic system where physically possible; grout the annular space; steel casing through the saprolite.
Water quality to test for at commissioningTotal coliform and E. coli, nitrate/nitrite, pH, hardness, iron and manganese (common and staining in Piedmont wells), radon in water (both counties sit on the granitic/gneissic rocks associated with radon), arsenic, lead, and uranium. Retest annually for bacteria.
Indicative cost$8,000–$25,000 drilled, cased, pumped and plumbed, depending on depth and whether rock is met shallow; ~$17,000 is a reasonable single-figure allowance at 250–300 ft. Estimate

Are raised beds advisable? Yes. Primarily to defeat the slope — terraced raised beds on contour give you level planting, stop the soil washing downhill, and keep nutrients out of the reservoir. Secondarily to fix pH and organic matter in a controlled volume. Yes — emphatically. Raised beds are the direct answer to 30-inch rock (you cannot dig deep anyway), to the expansive clay, and to the slow-draining group-C subsoil. Build up rather than down.
Is imported topsoil / compost needed? Yes. Budget bulk compost and topsoil for any bed, and plan annual compost top-dressing. Yes, and more of it — lower organic matter, lower surface pH, and rock limiting the effective rooting depth.
A site-specific warning Everything applied on this lot drains into a public drinking-water reservoir at 17.9% grade. Fertiliser and manure management is not merely good practice here — the watershed ordinance exists precisely to control this. Favour compost over soluble fertiliser, keep soil covered, and never leave bare earth on the slope. K = 0.43 means bare silt loam will move in the first hard rain. Mulch continuously; the covenants also impose a $1,000 penalty per tree removed, so clearing for a garden needs Association approval first.

Both properties: get a soil test before buying a single amendment. UGA Cooperative Extension soil tests cost roughly $12–$20 through the county Extension office and return pH, lime requirement, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, manganese and zinc for the actual sample. Nothing in SSURGO substitutes for it — SSURGO describes a map unit, not your garden. Soil test recommended before amendment

18Gardening and farming — what will actually grow

Both sites are humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa) with near-identical growing seasons — 236 days at A, 233 at B (32 °F threshold) — so the plant lists are largely shared. The meaningful differences are the half-zone split (A = USDA 8a, B = 8b), A's south-facing 18% slope (more heat, faster drainage, frost drains away downslope) and B's north aspect with 30-inch rock (cooler, moister, shallow rooting). Verdict on growing Both properties will grow a great deal, and neither will do it without work. They share a ~235-day growing season, a half-zone apart, on the classic Georgia Piedmont profile of thin acid topsoil over heavy clay. Property A's advantages are better drainage, a full-sun south aspect, frost drainage downslope, and ideal conditions for Mediterranean herbs and fruit trees; its problems are the slope, which forces terracing, and its position above a drinking-water reservoir, which constrains fertiliser practice. Property B's advantages are twice the land, level ground, better nutrient retention and moisture, and a warmer zone (8b) that opens pomegranate and jujube; its problems are 30-inch rock capping rooting depth, expansive clay, slow drainage and a covenant regime that polices tree removal. Raised beds are the correct answer at both.

26Dock feasibility

Property A — no private dock. This is as close to settled as a negative gets. Three converging official facts:
  1. CCWA owns the bed, the shoreline and the upland strip — a private owner has no riparian interest to build from.
  2. Zoning Sec. 4.5(D)(3) bars any "substantial structure, or other feature which may adversely impact the reservoir" within the 150-ft buffer — which encompasses the entire shoreline area.
  3. CCWA Rule 5 confines all reservoir access to the entrance gate, and Sec. 4.5(D)(4) subordinates all reservoir access to CCWA policy.
No CCWA document authorises private docks and no dock permit programme appears to exist. Official for the three underlying rules

The state rule is worth understanding because it shows the decision was CCWA's to make. Ga. Rule 391-3-16-.01(8)(b) provides that swimming, fishing, boating, docks, public access and adjacent property owner access are "permissible in the reservoir management plan if the water quality of the reservoir is adequately protected." So docks are permitted in principle by the State — and CCWA has elected not to allow them. The operative document is CCWA's DNR-approved reservoir management plan, which is not published online. › Request it from CCWA in writing, and get the dock answer in writing, before paying any premium for "dock potential." Plan not retrieved
Property B — new private docks are possible on Thurmond Lake, but two hard gates stand in the way, and we could not clear either for Lots 130/131 Governing document: Shoreline Management Plan for J. Strom Thurmond Lake Project, Georgia and South Carolina, USACE Savannah District Pamphlet DP 1130-2-11, effective 1 May 2018. Official

There is no lake-wide moratorium. The only use of "moratorium" in the SMP is a penalty against a non-compliant permittee (¶12.h), not a freeze. What actually limits docks is shoreline allocation plus a 2018 policy change:

Gate 1 — allocation. Which colour applies to the shoreline in front of Lots 130/131 could NOT be determined. Not found The eight 2018 allocation map sheets are raster images with no extractable data, and USACE itself says the maps are reference only: "To determine the shoreline allocation adjacent to a particular site, please contact the Thurmond Project Office, toll free, at 800-533-3478." Note that Protected Shoreline is used specifically for water too shallow for navigation, subject to siltation or rapid dewatering — i.e. back-of-cove shallows are a classic yellow designation, and that is exactly the setting here.

Gate 2 — the plat date. SMP ¶16.a: "Only community docks will be authorized in all new county certified, platted subdivisions approved after implementation of this plan" (1 May 2018). The Declaration was recorded in 2006, which suggests the subdivision predates it — but the plat, or any replat, of the Watersedge Cove phase must be dated from the Lincoln County plat book. If that phase was certified after 1 May 2018, no individual dock will ever be permitted on these lots. Official Plat date not obtained

Ask for a written shoreline allocation determination and request a ranger field inspection before purchase — USACE explicitly encourages prospective buyers to do this.
Property B — full private-dock requirements under the 2018 SMP Official
Eligibility (¶14)Must own in fee simple private property adjacent to public land zoned Limited Development. Minimum 20 ft of common frontage with LD-zoned public land. Shallow "finger"/"flag" lots do not qualify even if they meet the 20 ft. No easement access — applications are not accepted where access to public land is via an easement from a private owner. Proof of access = recorded deed and plat. No permits in wetlands or culturally/archaeologically sensitive areas; none to minors.
The 90° projection surveyA perpendicular projection from the shared private/public boundary determines usable frontage. "If the 90° projection bisects or crosses other frontage areas, previously permitted areas, or private property before reaching the 330' msl, the property will not qualify for shoreline use permits." Survey must be by a state-licensed surveyor at 1 inch = 100 feet.
The two-lot trap (¶14.d)If one structure (house, garage) or supporting feature (driveway, pool, porch) occupies more than one lot, the lots are treated as ONE lot and qualify for ONE permit only. Permits already issued are cancelled and the surplus facilities must be removed. › If you buy both lots and build a single house or driveway spanning them, you forfeit the second dock right.
One dock per lot (¶15)One private floating facility per separate property, where "separate" means professionally surveyed, platted by a licensed surveyor and recorded as distinct in the county courthouse or tax office.
No speculation (¶12.e)"Permits and/or licenses will not be issued for commercial or speculative purposes in order to enhance the selling potential of adjacent private property." A seller cannot obtain a permit to make a lot marketable.
Dock size (¶15.a)Flat-T, no slip: max 200 sq ft, min 100 sq ft, no side under 6 ft. With slip(s): max 720 sq ft total footprint. Sun decks, jet-ski lifts and staircases all count. Must be certified by a licensed professional engineer. Enclosed structures of any kind not authorised; no human habitation; houseboats and seaplanes may not be moored at private docks.
Spacing (¶15.c)Minimum 50-ft buffer from any existing facility or mooring buoy, measured at 330' msl. Dock plus walkway must not extend more than one-third across a cove. No "crossover" placements. A ranger decides placement and may require shallower water. Where two docks cannot both meet spacing — "small coves or narrow lots" — it is first-come, first-served.
Water depth (¶15.d)There is NO numeric minimum. The standard is qualitative: sufficient depth "to be serviceable for at least a part of the recreation season." If approved in a shallow spot a Special Condition records that the applicant knew. In low water, owners may "chase water" temporarily.
Permit term & transferUp to 5 years, non-transferable. Automatically revoked on sale or transfer of the adjacent property, sale of the facility, or death of the holder and spouse. New owner must apply within 14 days or remove the facility and restore the area within 14 days. Some facilities are "grandfathered" to the present owner only and must be removed on sale.
Fees (published 5-year rates)Floating facility (dock) $30.00; electric line $35; water line $35; improved walkway $50; underbrushing with a dock free, alone $10; shoreline protection free. No annual fee in this schedule. The current fee table is a scanned image with no extractable text, so amounts are unverified — confirm with the project office. A separate USACE Real Estate Licence is required for improved walkways, electrical and water lines, dock gangwalks and anchors.

Partial applications are not accepted. First-time applicants for new facilities must meet on site with a Ranger. Processing ~2–4 weeks. Appeal within 30 days to the District Commander. Filing: J. Strom Thurmond Project, ATTN: Shoreline Section, Rt. 1 Box 12, Clarks Hill, SC 29821.

Post-1 May 2018 subdivisions: community docks ONLY, typically max 2 slips per 82 ft of LD shoreline, with the HOA deciding which lots get moorage. Existing subdivisions: generally one slip per 70 ft of dockable boundary. This section is the heart of the comparison Property A's water body is, for recreational purposes, closed. No gas motor, no boat over 20 ft, no swimming, no launching from your land, no dock, no shoreline access, five days a week for eight months of the year, on a paid ticket through a gate. It is a beautiful view and a place to paddle a canoe on a Saturday in April. It is not a lake lifestyle, and anyone buying it as one will be disappointed.

Property B's water body is the real thing — 71,100 acres, 1,200 miles of shoreline, no horsepower limits, year-round, free to access, with marinas and a nationally regarded striper fishery. The entire question is whether this particular lot can reach it with a dock, and nobody but USACE can answer that.

The Georgia radon programme (via UGA Cooperative Extension) publishes test summaries but we could not obtain verified county average pCi/L figures from a primary state source. Third-party aggregators quote a Georgia statewide average near 7 pCi/L; that figure is unverified, self-selected-sample data and should not be relied on.
EPA's own caveats matter here, and so does the geology The map was built in 1993 and EPA states plainly: "The Map of Radon Zones should not be used to determine if individual homes need to be tested" and "All homes should be tested, regardless of zone designation." Fix at >=4 pCi/L; consider fixing between 2 and 4. EPA directs users to USGS Open-File Report 93-292-D for intra-county variation, which matters because a single county-wide zone masks local geology.

Both lots sit on granitic/gneissic Piedmont rock — the lithology most associated with elevated indoor radon in Georgia (§42). For Property A in particular, Zone 2 status plus that bedrock makes passive radon-resistant new construction (RRNC) a sensible specification: a sub-slab vent mat, sealed membrane and capped vertical stack cost little at framing and are expensive to retrofit. Test after occupancy and activate the stack with a fan only if needed. Our recommendation

Also note the radon-in-water angle if a well is ever used (§16) — Piedmont crystalline aquifers can carry dissolved radon, and it is a standard commissioning test.

42Sinkholes, karst and geology

Neither property is karst terrain. Sinkhole risk is negligible at both. Confirmed three ways.
  1. Direct bedrock identification at Property A. A geologic point query at the parcel's interior coordinate returns map unit "Biotitic Gneiss / Mica Schist / Amphibolite," lithology amphibolite + biotite gneiss + mica schist, age Precambrian to Paleozoic, from the Georgia Geological Survey Digital Geologic Map of Georgia (v.2, 1999, 1:500,000). These are hard, crystalline, non-soluble metamorphic rocks — the classic Piedmont assemblage. Official
  2. Aquifer coding confirms it independently. Every USGS NWIS groundwater site with an assigned national aquifer code in both counties returns N400PDMBRX — the Piedmont and Blue Ridge crystalline-rock aquifer. No carbonate aquifer is recorded in either county. That is about as direct as documentary evidence of non-karst geology gets. Official
  3. USGS karst criteria exclude the Piedmont. The national karst compilation maps karst to soluble bedrock — carbonate and evaporite rocks, or low-viscosity volcanics. Georgia's genuine karst is confined to the Valley and Ridge in the far northwest (Walker, Catoosa, Dade, Chattooga) and the Coastal Plain limestones of the southwest (the Dougherty Plain around Albany). The Piedmont province, which contains both counties, is not karst. Official — USGS criteria County-scale polygon not read directly
QuestionProperty AProperty B
Known sinkholesNone — not karst terrainNone — not karst terrain
Sinkhole reportsNone foundNone found; the Lincoln County multi-hazard mitigation plan has zero mentions of sinkhole or karst
Karst geologyAbsentAbsent
Nearby subsidenceNone foundNone found

Ruling out sinkholes does not rule out geotechnical trouble — the opposite problem applies Piedmont crystalline terrain has its own well-known characteristics, and both lots have them:
  • Saprolite. Bedrock weathers in place to deep clayey residual soil, and depth to competent rock varies dramatically over short distances — 10 ft in one boring, 60 ft in another 50 ft away. Plan multiple borings across the actual building footprint.
  • Shallow rock. The converse — rock near the surface drives up excavation cost for footings, basements, utility trenches and especially septic trenches. Georgia denies conventional septic permits where rock is less than 24 in below the proposed field.
  • Perched groundwater and seeps at the saprolite/rock interface, common on lake-adjacent slopes, affecting basement waterproofing and drainfield suitability alike.
  • Radon — these are exactly the lithologies associated with it (§41).
Budget for possible rock. Do not budget for sinkholes.

Three things this table is easy to misread 1 The county ratings invert at tract level, and the tract is the relevant geography. Property A's tract scores Relatively Low overall with Relatively Low social vulnerability — the panhandle is the best-situated part of Clayton County. Property B's tract scores Relatively Moderate, the higher-risk of Lincoln County's two tracts, with Relatively High social vulnerability.
2 Lincoln County actually experiences MORE of several hazards per year than Clayton — more tornado segments (0.158 vs 0.095), more strong-wind events (3.56 vs 2.67), more heat waves, more winter weather, and far more drought (60.9 vs 39.2). It rates "Very Low" because there is little insured value in the path. Do not read Lincoln's "Very Low" composite as "safer for my house."
3 Both counties rate "Very Low" on community resilience (bottom ~10–14% nationally) — a genuine shared negative measuring capacity to absorb and recover from a disaster.
Historical tornado record — NOAA Storm Prediction Center database, 1950–2024 (71,813 US records analysed by county FIPS) Official
A Clayton County11 segments, 1967–2021: 5 × F0, 3 × F1, 3 × F2, no F3+. 113 injuries, 2 fatalities. The significant event is 31 Mar 1973, F2, 72.4-mile path, 500 yd wide, 100 injuries, 2 deaths. Note a recent cluster — 2019, 2020 and 2021, three consecutive years.
B Lincoln County9 segments, 1998–2013: 5 × F0, 2 × F1, 2 × F2, no F3+. 8 injuries, no fatalities. Both F2s fell on 7 May 1998, a single outbreak day — the county's multi-hazard plan records a 4-tornado F1/F2 outbreak that day destroying 19 homes in two subdivisions, and a maximum historical F3 in Nov 1992. The record starting in 1998 almost certainly reflects reporting bias in a sparsely populated county, so the true long-run rate is probably higher than the 0.12/yr observed — FEMA's 0.158/yr supports that.
Hail & wind damageLincoln County's 2020 Multi-Hazard Plan records 97 thunderstorm-wind events / $318k and 51 hail events / only $12k of damage. Hail is a real roof-replacement risk at Property A (5.47 events/yr county-wide) and moderate at B. Specify an impact-resistant Class 3–4 roof covering at both; at B the covenant-driven metal roof is well suited.
WildfireGeorgia Forestry Commission, Lincoln County 1957–2018: 1,245 events, 4,895 acres, averaging 3.9 acres — frequent but small, in a wildland–urban-interface setting. Maintain defensible space on a wooded lot at either property.
Design conclusionRelatively High tornado risk at both tracts, and neither county has ever recorded an EF3+ in 75 years. A reinforced interior safe room is worth costing on either lot — we allow $9,000 in §Cost. Pair it with an impact-resistant roof and, at A, passive radon-resistant construction.

The counter-intuitive result, and why it holds The smaller house on the cheaper land costs about $107,000 more — $65/SF more. The drivers, in order of size:
  1. Fixed site costs spread over less floor area — $43/SF of site cost at B vs $31/SF at A
  2. Rural mobilisation premium — roughly $59,000 of pure location penalty
  3. Longer driveway, water line and power run, plus a propane system that A does not need
  4. Covenant-mandated premium materials — standing-seam metal roof, ~900 sq ft of deep porch
  5. Higher overhead, profit and contingency, justified by a thin bidder pool and the hard 15-month completion deadline
Property A's own cost drivers — $52,000 of grading and $38,000 of retaining walls, $90,000 between them — are real, but they are smaller than B's cumulative rural and covenant penalties.

The honest conclusion on building Building a 5-bedroom custom home is value-destructive on both lots, and roughly twice as badly on Property B. This is not a criticism of either property; it is the ordinary arithmetic of custom building in markets where finished-home prices sit well below replacement cost.

In Waterpointe, $541,000–$565,000 already buys a finished large home against $833,600 to build one — a saving of roughly $280,000 for substantially the same product. If the objective is a large house at or near its cost, buy an existing Waterpointe home rather than build.

The cases where building still makes sense are specific and worth naming: you want something that does not exist in the local stock; you intend to hold for 15+ years so the premium amortises; the lake view or the specific lot has irreplaceable personal value; or you can act as your own general contractor and capture the $132,000–$152,000 of builder overhead and profit. If none of those is true, the numbers say buy, not build.

Final due-diligence summary

56Property strengths — documented advantages only

Property A

  • Location & accessibility. ATL international airport 21 mi / 43 min with ~220 nonstops and a rail link; general-aviation field 20 min.
  • Schools at the door. Elementary and middle both 1.8 mi; high school 3.8 mi.
  • Healthcare. Full ED 22 min, four EDs within 35 min, Level I trauma 45 min, urgent care 12 min, pharmacy 13 min.
  • Services. Grocery 2.9 mi, Walmart 4.3 mi, hardware 4.9 mi — 3×–10× closer than B on every category.
  • South Asian community. Hindu Temple of Atlanta 17.7 mi / 32 min in the same county; 3 Indian restaurants within 30 min; 15,000–30,000 Asian Indian residents within an hour.
  • An affluent, stable immediate area. Tract median household income $119,872, owner-occupancy 90.8%, family households 88.8% — a market that can support a premium home.
  • Low hazard at tract level — Relatively Low composite risk, Relatively Low social vulnerability, lowest-but-two flood exposure of 22 Clayton tracts.
  • Flood. Zone X, minimal hazard, no BFE, 8.6 ft above the water at its lowest point.
  • Lot qualifies on the hard tests. 57,954 sq ft and ~416 ft deep — clears both of Sec. 4.5(D)'s numeric thresholds, with margin.
  • Real amenities. HOA pool, tennis courts and clubhouse — and membership is voluntary, with unbuilt-lot dues contractually capped at $100/yr.
  • Building potential. ~30,000–33,000 sq ft envelope, 20,280 sq ft impervious allowance; the slope makes a daylight basement with a lake view nearly free architecturally.
  • Hobby farming. Up to 12 hens permitted by a dedicated county ordinance — the only one of the two lots where any poultry is possible.
  • Low shrink–swell soil (LEP 1.5%) and a 50-in weathered — not indurated — rock contact.
  • Mains water almost certainly at the road, with published 2026 rates.

Property B

  • A genuinely usable lake. Clarks Hill / Thurmond is 71,100 acres with ~1,200 miles of shoreline, no motor or horsepower restrictions, open year-round and free to access, with six marinas and many public ramps. This is the single largest advantage either property holds over the other.
  • Terrain. In-lot average grade 3.7% (2.1°), max 7.3% over 50 ft, relief 34.5 ft over 2.14 acres — genuinely gently sloping, exactly as advertised. Minimal grading, no retaining walls, slab or crawlspace both feasible.
  • Price and size. 2.14 acres for $55,000 — twice the land for less than half A's asking price. ~$25,700/acre.
  • Possible owner financing — advertised by the seller on the HOA classifieds.
  • Two separate recorded lots, which preserves optionality (resell one, or — subject to the ¶14.d trap — two dock rights).
  • Small schools. Ratios 13.6–15.5 and a high school of 367 against Lovejoy's 2,136.
  • Fishing. Nationally regarded striped bass and hybrid fishery, stocked by GA and SC DNR, with a Georgia licence covering the whole impoundment under the reciprocal agreement.
  • Recreation. Three state parks within 42–81 min; Elijah Clark SP 21.4 mi.
  • Quiet. No speedway, no metro traffic, no through traffic.
  • Flood. Zone X, minimal hazard, no BFE, 26 ft above full pool.
  • Radon Zone 3 — the lowest EPA band, against A's Zone 2.
  • Rentals are permitted by the covenants with no minimum term and no STR ban.
  • A favourable alternative soil on site. Cecil (CeB) is rated "Not limited" for dwellings and only "Somewhat limited" for septic — if the field lands there.
  • Paved roads and underground utilities within the subdivision.

Closing statement of limitations This report is a screening and decision-support document. It is not a survey, an appraisal, a legal opinion, an engineering certification, a floodplain determination, or a soil evaluation.

Every elevation, contour, slope, area and distance derived from the lidar DEM or from county GIS is marked GIS-derived and is model-based. Parcel geometry for Property A comes from a county service that Clayton County itself disclaims as "not a true and exact representation of property boundaries." Property B's boundary is our reconstruction from listing dimensions and road geometry, because no plat or parcel polygon is publicly obtainable.

The following require a licensed professional or an agency determination and must not be taken from this report: boundary and topographic surveys; septic design, bedroom capacity and perc results; foundation and retaining-wall design; grading quantities; floodplain or elevation certification; dock eligibility; zoning verification; and the content of unread covenants.

Where we could not confirm something we have written Not found rather than estimating it. There are 27 such items in §58 and they are the most important part of this document — the next step is not more desk research, it is the four starred phone calls.
